assumptions: Smaller responsible operators are permitted and willing to outsource the relevant hosting and evidence operations.
Final technical and backup requirements do not impose prohibitive certification or capital burdens.
Paid readiness work can reveal a repeatable schema rather than mostly bespoke ERP integration.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid readiness engagements with covered operators, verified implementation effort and gross margin, written confirmation of provider requirements, conversion to hosting contracts, supplier-data completeness metrics, and a signed lab or consultant referral channel.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A decentralized passport regime leaves responsible operators needing an operational evidence, hosting, and registry bridge rather than merely a registry record.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A hard market-access deadline creates meaningful willingness to pay, but outsourcing preference among smaller CEE operators and supplier-data pain are unvalidated.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Implementation fees plus prepaid recurring hosting can generate attractive margins and continuity, though ERP-specific onboarding, security, support, certification, CAC, and account counts are assumptions.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish and CEE smaller producers and importers form a plausible niche, but addressable account count, concentration, and relevant battery categories are unknown.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Localized managed onboarding may win underserved accounts, but established DPP, ERP, and PLM vendors have stronger integrations, trust, and bundling power.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Winning battery workflows could support additional battery categories, supplier evidence services, other product passports, and broader CEE coverage.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Schema libraries, evidence history, and record continuity create some switching costs, but the company lacks exclusive access and the workflow remains replaceable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Polish-language managed exception handling can improve convenience for smaller operators, but superiority over established platforms has not been demonstrated.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: The February 2027 mandate creates a near-term, non-discretionary readiness window and recurring maintenance need.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Testing labs and compliance consultants are sensible channels, but there are no signed partners, producer relationships, or proven acquisition costs.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A readiness-service wedge is feasible within capital limits, while production hosting requires authoritative data, registry compatibility, security, legal reliability, and potentially demanding ERP integrations.

highest_value_structural_change: Secure an authoritative compliance-lab partnership and standard connector for one concentrated battery niche before broadening into generic DPP hosting.
main_structural_strength: A hard near-term market-access deadline supports a high-value implementation event followed by recurring data maintenance and hosting.
primary_score_limiter: The business has no producer access or integration rights and must compete against trusted DPP, ERP, and PLM vendors under unsettled service-provider requirements.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Large operators can extend existing systems, while certification and backup obligations may structurally favor established vendors.
